record.paper_title: Open questions on defining and computing the vapour-liquid surface tension by virial and test transformation approaches
record.original_question: What causes the disagreement between surface tensions of spherical vapour-liquid interfaces computed by the standard virial route and by the test-area or test-transformation method, and can an infinitesimal test-area limit that includes a second-order virial term make the two approaches agree? A self-contained resolution must explain whether spherical distortions require both the variance of the energy response and a contribution involving second derivatives of the pair potential, because ordinary virial-route methods for spheres account only for first derivatives of the potential.

evidence.quote: Unfortunately, results for the surface tension of droplets and bubbles from the virial route are known to disagree both with results from test transformations (test area method) and with what is known about the Tolman length for the respective systems. In particular, the surface tension of Lennard-Jones nanodroplets is significantly smaller if computed by the virial route than by the test area method [1]; other thermodynamic methods tend to agree with the test area results [2].

The results disagree with those from the virial route to such an extent that fixing the discrepancy just through the definition of the radius would lead to using an unreasonable dividing surface [1]. So, for our purposes, the main immediate aim is to figure out what makes the two methods disagree so much, and what else can be attempted in order to make them agree.

We can take the same limit for the spherical test area method; it will give us a virial expression that, by design, must agree with the test area method. Based on the above, we can expect it to contain a second-order expression that was absent for planar interfaces, and that is indeed the case.

The third term,β3(q, q′), contains a second derivative of the pair potential. This contribution has been overlooked by all virial-route methods for spheres so far, since through forces acting between moleculesi and j, withf ℓij = −∂uij/∂r ℓij, they were only accounting for first derivatives of uij. To be consistent with the test area method, however, we need to include a term that contains the derivative of the force.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a classical fluid of $N$ point particles in three-dimensional space interacting through a smooth pairwise potential $u(r)$, in a thermodynamic state that supports a stable spherical vapour–liquid interface (a droplet or a bubble) at temperature $T$. Two routes are commonly used to assign a surface tension $\gamma$ to such a curved interface:

(1) The standard virial (mechanical) route for spherical geometries, which expresses $\gamma$ as an integral over differences of normal and tangential components of the pressure tensor, with the tangential pressure built from the pair forces $f_{ij}^{\ell}=-\partial u(r_{ij})/\partial r_{ij}^{\ell}$ — i.e. only from first derivatives of $u$.

(2) The test-area (test-transformation) route, which defines $\gamma$ from the free-energy response to an infinitesimal area-preserving deformation of the interface; for a deformation parameter $\xi$ with energy change $\Delta U(\xi)$, the canonical free-energy expansion gives
$$\Delta F = \langle \Delta U\rangle - \frac{1}{2T}\,\mathrm{Var}(\Delta U) + O(\xi^{3}),$$
and $\gamma$ is identified with the coefficient of the change in surface area.

Question. For a spherical interface, take the infinitesimal limit of the test-area expression and rewrite it as a virial-type ensemble average. Show that the resulting expression contains, in addition to the usual first-derivative virial contribution $\beta_{1}$ and an energy-variance contribution $\beta_{2}$, a third term $\beta_{3}(q,q')$ that depends on the second derivatives of the pair potential $u$ (equivalently, on the derivative of the pair force). Prove that:

(a) For planar interfaces this second-derivative term vanishes, so the virial and test-area routes coincide.

(b) For spherical interfaces the second-derivative term is generically non-zero, and including it makes the infinitesimal-limit virial expression identically equal to the test-area surface tension.

(c) Hence the long-standing numerical disagreement between the spherical virial route and the test-area method (for example, for Lennard-Jones nanodroplets, where the virial route yields a markedly smaller $\gamma$) is fully attributable to the omission of this second-order, second-derivative contribution, rather than to ambiguities in the choice of dividing surface.

Provide either a proof of (a)–(c) or a counterexample showing that an additional contribution beyond $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}$ is required to reconcile the two routes.
artifact.status_search_result: The reconciliation of the spherical virial route with the test-area method via inclusion of a second-derivative (second-order virial) term is presented as one of several explicitly open questions on computing vapour–liquid surface tension. No subsequent work establishing rigorous equivalence or a complete numerical resolution for curved interfaces (e.g. Lennard-Jones nanodroplets) has been located.

status_evidence.title: Open questions on defining and computing the vapour-liquid surface tension
status_evidence.snippet: Addresses problems including the disagreement between spherical virial and test-area methods; introduces a second-order virial term containing second derivatives of the pair potential.
status_evidence.claim: The discrepancy and its proposed second-derivative resolution are framed as an open question.

status_evidence.title: Calculation of surface tension via area sampling
status_evidence.snippet: Test-area method for surface tension; documents disagreement with virial route for curved interfaces.
status_evidence.claim: Disagreement between virial and test-area routes for spherical interfaces is a known, unresolved issue.
